title: Airbnb's growth spurt comes with a catch
detail:
Airbnb's growth spurt comes with a catch
Tobi Opeyemi Amure, Celine Provini
Sun, November 8, 2026 at 9:07 AM CST 4 min read
ABNB
Trade Airbnb on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Booking a vacation rental used to mean paying up front.

You found the place, entered your card and hoped your plans held. If they didn't, you were stuck chasing a refund.

Airbnb (ABNB) changed that math this year, and travelers noticed. Revenue rose 19% to $4.9 billion in the third quarter, its fastest growth in three years, according to Skift.

CEO Brian Chesky has called pricing "a massive lever" for growth, Rental Scale-Up reported.

However, a subtle shift has emerged in how Airbnb is earning that growth.

According to a Deutsche Bank research report seen by TheStreet, a meaningful slice of Airbnb's acceleration came from its Reserve Now, Pay Later program, even as the core business also sped up.

Airbnb's pay-later bookings did a lot of the lifting

The numbers were strong across the board.

Nights and seats booked rose 16% to 155 million, up from 10% growth in the second quarter, Rental Scale-Up reported. Gross booking value climbed 21% to $27.7 billion.

Deutsche Bank analyst Benjamin Black broke down where that growth came from in a Nov. 6 note titled "Growth is Back in the Neighborhood."

Related: KeyBanc says consider buying shares of popular travel giant now

"RNPL [Reserve Now, Pay Later] provided 3ppt of net nights growth in 3Q, versus approximately 1.5ppt in 2Q, but the underlying business also accelerated," wrote Black.

By my math, pay-later bookings accounted for nearly a fifth of Airbnb's 16% growth. Without them, nights would have grown about 13%.

Hotels added less than a point, Black wrote. That suggests "core homes growth reached approximately 12%," he added.

Black kept his Buy rating and raised his price target to $220 from $200. The stock closed at $170.13 on Nov. 5, the note showed. By my math, that target implies about 29% upside.

Airbnb bookings jumped 16% as pay-later gained traction, despite cancellations rising to 19% and Deutsche Bank seeing upside.Jose A. Bernat Bacete / Getty Images
More travelers are canceling

Pay-later bookings come with a trade-off.

Airbnb's cancellation rate rose to about 19% from about 16% a year earlier, Rental Scale-Up reported. The company's filings say pay-later bookings cancel more often than bookings paid up front.

CFO Ellie Mertz called that rate "very healthy in the travel space," the outlet reported.

Guests on the program aren't charged until eight days before their free-cancellation deadline. On Airbnb's strictest Firm policy, that's about 38 days before check-in.

If you book this way, I'd put that charge date in your calendar. Your card gets hit weeks before the trip, and missing the cancellation window can cost you the full stay.

title: Airbnb: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors
detail:
Airbnb: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors
The Motley Fool Team, The Motley Fool
Sun, November 8, 2026 at 2:08 AM CST 3 min read
ABNB
Trade Airbnb on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 5, 2026, Airbnb (NASDAQ:ABNB) announced revenue of $4.9 billion and expanding night volumes across all core markets. For long-term investors, the key issue is whether structural efficiency gains and platform expansions can support lasting profit growth. Three things management said stand out.

1. Boutique Hotel Listings Drive Traffic and Funnel Guests to Core Homes

Adding hotels expands options for short stays without diluting platform identity. Hotel listings bring first-time users into the ecosystem, and a substantial portion eventually books residential properties.

In fact, approximately 35% of guests whose first booking is a hotel, they come back and they book a home within a year.
-- Brian Chesky, Co-Founder and Chief Executive Officer

2. Automated Support Tools Lower Unit Costs While Expanding Margins

Deploying artificial intelligence software to resolve routine guest inquiries improves operational efficiency without expanding headcount. Lower support expenses preserve capital while supporting higher profitability as total booking volumes increase.

What this means is that customer support cost per booking has declined more than 17% year-over-year, driven in large part by improvements to our AI assistant.
-- Brian Chesky, Co-Founder and Chief Executive Officer

3. Share Buyback Expansion Capitalizes on Robust Free Cash Flow Generation

Substantial cash generation allows management to return capital directly to shareholders. Expanding share repurchases signals balance sheet confidence while reducing total share count over time.

Finally, during Q3, we repurchased $700 million of our common stock, enabled by our strong balance sheet and significant cash flow generation, leaving $2.7 billion remaining under our existing authorization. And today, we're pleased to announce Board approval of a new $12 billion share repurchase program on top of this existing authorization.
-- Ellie Mertz, Chief Financial Officer

Looking Ahead

Accelerating booking volume across international markets reflects operational momentum, giving leadership space to expand secondary services. Management relies on proprietary listing density, direct host communication, and flexible payment arrangements to maintain marketplace liquidity. Executives prioritize overall booking momentum and full-year margin expansion.

Airbnb is back in growth mode. It's rare for a marketplace of our size to reaccelerate growth, but that's exactly what we're doing. Q3 was our fastest revenue growth in more than 3 years.
-- Brian Chesky, Co-Founder and Chief Executive Officer

detail:
Airbnb Just Popped After a Blowout Quarter. Is the Stock Still a Buy?
Matt Frankel, CFP®, The Motley Fool
Sat, November 7, 2026 at 7:02 AM CST 5 min read
ABNB
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Airbnb (NASDAQ:ABNB) shares jumped by 12% on Friday after the company reported third-quarter results that handily beat expectations. The stock is now just under its 52-week high and has gained 40% so far in 2026.

For the past few years, the general consensus among investors has been that Airbnb is a great business. It's just not growing at a rate that anyone would consider impressive. But the company's third-quarter results could change that perception.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

A blowout quarter with a lot to like

Airbnb's revenue grew 19% year-over-year, or 16% excluding any currency effects, which was significantly higher than analysts were expecting. On the bottom line, earnings per share were $3.16, compared to the $2.85 expectation among Wall Street analysts.

Demand was extremely strong as well. Nights and seats booked through the platform reached 155 million, up 16% from a year ago, and gross booking value grew 21% to $27.7 billion. Plus, the company remains an absolute cash machine. Airbnb has generated $4.9 billion in free cash flow over the past 12 months, and adjusted EBITDA increased by 22%.

The company is also starting to explore new growth areas and gain traction in some. Airbnb recently began adding adjacent services such as meal delivery and car rentals, and traditional hotels now account for a significant (but still single-digit) share of booked nights. These are all small pieces of Airbnb's revenue today, but they provide Airbnb with credible pathways to maintaining an elevated growth rate.

Looking ahead, management expects Airbnb's fourth-quarter revenue to fall in the range of $3.22-$3.28 billion, representing 17% growth at the midpoint.

Putting its cash to work

Airbnb has over $12 billion in cash on its balance sheet and, as mentioned, is generating free cash flow of roughly $5 billion annually. Well, the board authorized a new $12 billion share repurchase program, and that's on top of the $2.7 billion left under the existing authorization. Even after Friday's pop, the new buyback alone represents more than 10% of Airbnb's market value.

It's worth noting that Airbnb uses these buybacks (in part) to offset dilution from stock-based compensation, and the share count has shrunk and should continue to do so.

A new $12 billion share repurchase authorization adds to the positive outlook, although valuation and slowing benefits from flexible payments remain considerations.

Thursday, Nov. 5, was one of the market's roughest sessions in years. The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.52%, its worst day since April 2025, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 dropped 6.36%, its steepest decline since March 2020. Selling was driven in part by fears that Democrats' midterm gains could slow the AI data center buildout, and chip stocks took the brunt, with the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ: SMH) falling by roughly 11%.

Airbnb (NASDAQ: ABNB) didn't escape entirely, slipping 3.5% to close at $170.13. But it held up far better than the broader tech market, and it was still up about 3.5% on the week and more than 25% year to date heading into its report. That relative strength made Airbnb's third-quarter earnings release even more interesting. Would the results justify the stock's outperformance and notable relative strength, or give investors a reason to lock in gains?

At least initially, the answer was clear. Shares jumped about 11% in after-hours trading to trade near $189, within roughly 2% of their 52-week high of $193.45.

Airbnb's Revenue and Booking Growth Accelerate

Airbnb's third-quarter revenue rose 19% to $4.87 billion, its fastest growth in more than three years and well ahead of the roughly $4.75 billion analysts expected. Earnings of $3.16 per share also beat the $2.85 consensus by 31 cents, though a lower tax provision flattered the year-over-year comparison.

The demand metrics were arguably more impressive. Gross booking value climbed 21% to $27.7 billion, while nights and seats booked rose 16% to 155 million, a sharp acceleration from 10% growth in the second quarter. About three percentage points of that came from the expansion of Airbnb's Reserve Now, Pay Later option. Even excluding that lift, nights booked grew about 13%, which still marked an acceleration from the prior quarter.

The strength was also broad-based. Every region posted double-digit growth in nights booked, North America grew at its fastest pace in four years, and nights booked through Airbnb's app rose 29% to account for 66% of the total.

Over the past year, Booking Holdings (BKNG) stock lost 17.5%, dividends included, compared with a 9.8% return for the S&P 500. This performance marked the worst return within a peer group of five that includes Meta Platforms, Airbnb, Expedia and Hyatt Hotels. The lag occurred even though Meta is the only company in the group that converts a larger share of sales into operating profit than Booking does. So what do Booking's rivals offer that Booking does not?

Booking Is More Profitable Than Airbnb But Grows Slower

Most competitors offer faster sales growth. Airbnb operates in the same hotel and resort industry and provides the starkest contrast. During the four fiscal quarters ended September 30, 2026, Booking retained 32.8% of its revenue as operating profit, compared with 22.5% at Airbnb. Yet Booking reported revenue growth of 8.0% over those quarters, which is about half of Airbnb's 16.7% pace. That figure is held down by a $900 million legal charge, linked to an FTC action, that cut third-quarter revenue.

Investors pay far less for that profit, pricing the stock at 16.8 times earnings compared with 34.9 for Airbnb. Meta Platforms generates nearly the exact same margin as Booking, but its revenue expanded 27.5%. Meta is the only other comparable company priced above Booking on an earnings basis.
